title: Understanding and cleaning data
kicker: ENCT 202 · Foundation of Data Science · Chapter 3
subtitle: Most of a data scientist’s time goes here: real data is missing, duplicated, mis-typed and on wildly different scales.

sections.title: Profiling a dataset
sections.body: Before changing anything, ask: how many rows and columns? what type is each? how many values are missing? what are the min, max, mean? are there duplicates? Quick profiling catches a column of ages containing −1 or 999 before a model learns from it.

questions.prompt: An age column has a maximum of 999. This is most likely…

choices.text: A sign of an excellent dataset.
A placeholder for “unknown”, to be treated as missing.

sections.title: Missing values
sections.body: Options: drop rows or columns (fine if few), impute with mean/median/mode, or model the missing value from others. Median is safer for skewed data. Adding a “was missing” flag preserves the information that it was absent.

worked.why: Ages: 20, 22, 24, —, 90. The median of the known ones.
Mean would be 39, dragged up by 90; fill with 23.

questions.prompt: Which fill is most robust for skewed income data?

problems.prompt: Values 4, 6, 8, —, 100: mean vs median imputation for the gap?
problems.answer: Mean of known = 29.5; median = 7. The median ignores the outlier 100.

sections.title: Outliers
sections.body: Flag a value if |z| > 3, or if it lies beyond 1.5·IQR from the quartiles. Then investigate: a typo is fixed, a real extreme is kept (or modelled separately). Never delete just because it is inconvenient.

sections.title: Scaling and encoding
sections.body: Distance-based and gradient-based methods are thrown off by features in different units (salary in lakhs vs age in years). Min–max: (x − min)/(max − min) maps to [0, 1]. Standardise: (x − μ)/σ. Categories become numbers by one-hot encoding (one 0/1 column per category), or by ordering for ordinals.

questions.prompt: Colour ∈ {red, green, blue} one-hot encoded gives…

sections.title: A cleaning pipeline
sections.body: A repeatable pipeline: load → fix types → remove duplicates → handle missing → treat outliers → encode → scale → split. Fit scalers on the training set only and apply them to the test set; fitting on all data leaks information.

questions.prompt: Computing the scaling mean using the test set is…

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The test set must stay unseen.

diagram("Raw data -> Fix types

Scale -> Clean data");

sections.title: Combining sources
sections.body: Datasets are merged by a key (join). Watch for duplicate keys, mismatched formats (“NP” vs “Nepal”), and inconsistent units. Validate counts before and after a join; an inner join loses unmatched rows, a left join keeps them with blanks.
